questions.q: Which of Elena Marsh's five requirements did NOT go cleanly on the first attempt?
options: Requirement 1, the two-entity enterprise structure
Requirement 3, supplier/customer/bank/asset master data
Requirement 5, a clean first month-end close
Requirement 2, the chart of accounts design
questions.explain: Requirement 5, a clean month-end close, only became true after the full investigation and correction cycle in Chapter 3 — it did not succeed on the first attempt.

questions.q: What proved that the chart of accounts' intercompany design (Requirement 2) actually worked, beyond just being configured?
options: A theoretical review with no real transactions
The fact that the unposted intercompany journal's absence was exactly what broke the close, and posting it fixed the close
A separate audit unrelated to this capstone
Running the depreciation program
questions.explain: The intercompany design was proven under real pressure: its absence (the unposted journal) directly caused a close failure, and resolving it directly fixed it.

questions.q: What point does this lesson make about 'the system works' versus 'the requirement is met'?
options: They always mean exactly the same thing
A system can run every transaction without a single error and still fail to meet a requirement, like a clean close that needs full reconciliation
Requirements only matter before configuration begins
Once a system passes testing, requirements no longer need review
questions.explain: LTV's instance processed every transaction without a system error yet still failed the clean-close requirement on the first attempt, illustrating the gap between the two.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why is being honest about a requirement that didn't go cleanly on the first try actually a stronger interview answer?
options: Because interviewers prefer hearing about failures over successes
Because it demonstrates judgment: naming the real requirement, what was built, where it fell short, and how it was corrected
Because claiming perfection is always more convincing
Because it avoids discussing any technical detail
questions.explain: The lesson argues that showing where something didn't go cleanly and how it was fixed demonstrates real accountability and judgment, which is a stronger answer than claiming flawless execution.

questions.q: What does requirement 4, 'a full month of real transactions,' turn out to also be, according to this lesson?
options: Entirely separate from Chapter 3's crisis
Exactly where the six real problems entered the data, which is part of what real transactions look like
Unrelated to any of Elena Marsh's five requirements
A requirement that was never actually attempted in this capstone
questions.explain: The lesson candidly notes that running a real month of transactions is also exactly where the six planted problems entered the books — a realistic feature of real operations, not a flaw in the requirement.
